claim: The ClockΔ19 mutant behavioral phenotype is significantly modified by mouse strain genetic background.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the ClockΔ19 mutant behavioral phenotype is significantly modified by mouse strain genetic background.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: A suppressor of the ClockΔ19 mutation maps to a ~900 kb interval on mouse chromosome 1.
source: We map a suppressor of the ClockΔ19 mutation to a ∼900 kb interval on mouse chromosome 1 and identify the transcription factor, Usf1, as the responsible gene.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by mapping data in the results.

claim: Usf1 is the gene responsible for suppression of the ClockΔ19 mutation.
source: We map a suppressor of the ClockΔ19 mutation to a ∼900 kb interval on mouse chromosome 1 and identify the transcription factor, Usf1, as the responsible gene.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by multiple lines of evidence in the results including transgenic experiments.

claim: A SNP in the promoter of Usf1 causes elevation of its transcript and protein in strains that suppress the Clock mutant phenotype.
source: A SNP in the promoter of Usf1 causes elevation of its transcript and protein in strains that suppress the Clock mutant phenotype.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by promoter analysis and expression data in the results.

claim: USF1 competes with the CLOCK:BMAL1 complex for binding to E-box sites in target genes.
source: USF1 competes with the CLOCK:BMAL1 complex for binding to E-box sites in target genes.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by ChIP and EMSA data in the results.

claim: The CLOCKΔ19:BMAL1 complex has reduced affinity for E-box sites compared to wild-type CLOCK:BMAL1.
source: Saturation binding experiments demonstrate reduced affinity of the CLOCKΔ19:BMAL1 complex for E-box sites, thereby permitting increased USF1 occupancy on a genome-wide basis.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by saturation binding EMSA experiments in the results.

claim: Reduced affinity of CLOCKΔ19:BMAL1 permits increased USF1 occupancy on a genome-wide basis.
source: Saturation binding experiments demonstrate reduced affinity of the CLOCKΔ19:BMAL1 complex for E-box sites, thereby permitting increased USF1 occupancy on a genome-wide basis.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by ChIP-Seq data in the results.

claim: USF1 is an important modulator of molecular and behavioral circadian rhythms in mammals.
source: We propose that USF1 is an important modulator of molecular and behavioral circadian rhythms in mammals.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: The ClockΔ19 mutation was originally induced on the C57BL/6J isogenic background by ENU mutagenesis.
source: The mouse ClockΔ19 mutation was originally induced on the C57BL/6J (hereafter B6) isogenic background by ENU mutagenesis (Vitaterna et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section with a citation to previous work.

claim: ClockΔ19 lengthens circadian free-running period by about 1 hr in heterozygous mice.
source: ClockΔ19 lengthens circadian free-running period by about 1 hr in heterozygous mice, and by about 4 hr in homozygous mutant mice followed by arrhythmicity upon exposure to constant darkness (DD).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section describing the ClockΔ19 phenotype.

claim: ClockΔ19 lengthens circadian free-running period by about 4 hr in homozygous mutant mice followed by arrhythmicity upon exposure to constant darkness.
source: ClockΔ19 lengthens circadian free-running period by about 1 hr in heterozygous mice, and by about 4 hr in homozygous mutant mice followed by arrhythmicity upon exposure to constant darkness (DD).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section describing the ClockΔ19 phenotype.

claim: The circadian period phenotype in ClockΔ19/+ animals is suppressed by crossing to the BALB/cJ inbred strain.
source: We observed that the circadian period phenotype in ClockΔ19/+ animals is suppressed by crossing to the BALB/cJ (hereafter BALB) inbred strain.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: On an isogenic B6 background, ClockΔ19/+ lengthens period ~0.6 hr.
source: On an isogenic B6 background, ClockΔ19/+ lengthens period ∼0.6 hr, and this is suppressed to ∼0.3 hr on a (BALB x B6)F1 background.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section with specific quantitative data.

claim: The ClockΔ19/+ period lengthening is suppressed to ~0.3 hr on a (BALB x B6)F1 background.
source: On an isogenic B6 background, ClockΔ19/+ lengthens period ∼0.6 hr, and this is suppressed to ∼0.3 hr on a (BALB x B6)F1 background.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section with specific quantitative data.

claim: In ([BALB x B6]F1 x BALB)N4 mice, the ClockΔ19/+ period phenotype is completely suppressed.
source: In ([BALB x B6]F1 x BALB)N4 mice, the ClockΔ19/+ period phenotype is completely suppressed (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1A,B.

claim: At least one dominant suppressor allele exists in the BALB genome.
source: This suggests that at least one dominant suppressor allele exists in the BALB genome.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the suppression pattern observed in the crosses.

claim: The BALB suppression phenotype is tissue autonomous.
source: These results demonstrate that the BALB suppression phenotype is tissue autonomous and present in both central (SCN) and peripheral (pituitary) circadian clocks.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section based on tissue explant experiments.

claim: The BALB suppression phenotype is present in both central (SCN) and peripheral (pituitary) circadian clocks.
source: These results demonstrate that the BALB suppression phenotype is tissue autonomous and present in both central (SCN) and peripheral (pituitary) circadian clocks.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section based on tissue explant experiments.

claim: The circadian period in both ClockΔ19/+ SCN and pituitary was shorter in (BALB x B6)F1 animals than in mice of the B6 background.
source: The circadian period in both ClockΔ19/+ SCN and pituitary was shorter in (BALB x B6)F1 animals than in mice of the B6 background (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1C showing bioluminescence data.

claim: The BALB allele acts semidominantly to suppress the ClockΔ19 mutation.
source: Analysis of period in these crosses suggests that the BALB allele acts semidominantly to suppress the ClockΔ19 mutation.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the analysis of period distributions in different crosses.

claim: A significant association was detected between ClockΔ19 phenotype suppression and a locus on mouse chromosome 1, named Suppressor of Clock (Soc).
source: We performed QTL analysis on 222 (BALB x B6)F2 ClockΔ19/+ mice with 87 simple sequence length polymorphism markers (SSLP) and detected a significant association between ClockΔ19 phenotype suppression and a locus on mouse chromosome 1, which we named Suppressor of Clock (Soc) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by QTL mapping data in Figure 1E.

claim: Soc is physically located within the 165.1–190.45-Mb portion of mouse chromosome 1.
source: The congenic analysis demonstrates that Soc is physically located within the 165.1–190.45-Mb portion of mouse chromosome 1 and thus defines a genomic interval containing a new clock-related gene.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section based on congenic mapping.

claim: A significantly shorter free-running period was observed in ClockΔ19/+ animals from homozygous BALB Soc congenic lines than from ClockΔ19/+ littermates lacking the BALB allele.
source: We observed a significantly shorter free-running period in ClockΔ19/+ animals from homozygous BALB Soc congenic lines than from ClockΔ19/+ littermates lacking the BALB allele (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1F showing congenic analysis.

claim: The effect of Soc was significant on ClockΔ19/+ mutant, but not on wildtype or homozygous ClockΔ19 backgrounds.
source: The effect of Soc was significant on ClockΔ19/+ mutant, but not on wildtype or homozygous ClockΔ19 backgrounds.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section based on congenic analysis.

claim: Seven additional suppressor inbred strains were identified: A/J, AKR/J, C3H/HeJ, DBA/2J, FVB/NJ, SJL/J and 129S1/SvlmJ.
source: Of the 14 inbred strains tested, we identified seven additional suppressor and seven non-suppressor inbred strains (Figure 2A; Table 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 2A and Table 1.

claim: Seven non-suppressor inbred strains were identified: C58/J, BTBR T+tf/J, I/LnJ, MA/MyJ, JF1/Ms, MOLF/EiJ, and CZECHII/EiJ.
source: Of the 14 inbred strains tested, we identified seven additional suppressor and seven non-suppressor inbred strains (Figure 2A; Table 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 2A and Table 1.

claim: The Soc phenotype occurs as a consequence of shared ancestral alleles.
source: These results suggest that the Soc phenotype occurs as a consequence of shared ancestral alleles.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the strain distribution pattern.

claim: Soc maps to a 900-kb interval of chromosome 1 containing 22 candidate genes.
source: This region (green shading) spans 900 kb and contains 22 transcription units (Figure 2C; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 2C.

claim: The suppressor strains all carry haplotypes originating from M. domesticus.
source: The suppressor strains all carry haplotypes originating from M. domesticus and the non-suppressor strains all carry haplotypes originating from M. musculus–thus confirming our hypothesis of an ancestral allele.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section based on subspecific origin analysis.

claim: The non-suppressor strains all carry haplotypes originating from M. musculus.
source: The suppressor strains all carry haplotypes originating from M. domesticus and the non-suppressor strains all carry haplotypes originating from M. musculus–thus confirming our hypothesis of an ancestral allele.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section based on subspecific origin analysis.

claim: Seven Soc candidate genes (Vangl2, Usf1, Dcaf8, Copa, Pex19, Pea15, and Ncstn) expressed a similar pattern to the clock genes across 10 different tissues.
source: Via cluster analysis, we found that all nine clock genes expressed a similar pattern among the tissues examined (Figure 3A), but that only seven Soc candidates (Vangl2, Usf1, Dcaf8, Copa, Pex19, Pea15, and Ncstn) expressed a similar pattern to the clock genes.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 3A showing expression profiling.

claim: The ClockΔ19 mutation results from an A→T transversion in a splice donor site that causes exon skipping and disruption of the C-terminal transactivation domain of CLOCK.
source: The ClockΔ19 mutation results from an A→T transversion in a splice donor site that causes exon skipping and disruption of the C-terminal transactivation domain of CLOCK (King et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section with a citation to previous work.

claim: The levels of Per and Cry mRNA are much lower in ClockΔ19 mutants than in wild-type mice.
source: Consequently, the levels of Per and Cry mRNA are much lower in ClockΔ19 mutants than in wild-type mice (Lowrey and Takahashi, 2011).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section with a citation to previous work.

claim: Only Usf1 significantly activated transcription from both Per1 and Per2 E-boxes among the seven Soc candidates tested.
source: Of these, only Usf1 significantly activated transcription from both Per1 and Per2 E-boxes (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 3B showing transactivation assays.

claim: A dose response of Per promoter activation by USF1 was observed.
source: We observed a clear dose response of Per promoter activation by USF1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 3B.

claim: Activation of E-boxes by USF1 was not inhibited by the CRYs.
source: Unlike CLOCK:BMAL1, activation of E-boxes by USF1 was not inhibited by the CRYs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 3B showing transactivation assays.

claim: Only the Usf1 transcript exhibited significant up-regulation in F1 mice among the seven candidate genes tested in liver tissue.
source: Among the genes tested, only the Usf1 transcript exhibited significant up-regulation in F1 mice (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 3C showing qPCR data.

claim: USF1 protein levels in the liver were ~40% higher in BALB animals.
source: By western blot analysis, USF1 protein levels in the liver were ∼40% higher in BALB animals (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 3D showing western blot data.

claim: Significant up-regulation of Per1, Per2, Cry1 and Cry2 was detected in the F1 background.
source: We detected significant up-regulation of all four circadian genes tested in the F1 background (Figure 3E), consistent with elevated expression of an E-box transcription factor such as USF1.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 3E showing qPCR data.

claim: There are no coding mutations in Usf1 between the B6 and BALB mouse strains.
source: Because there are no coding mutations in Usf1 between the B6 and BALB mouse strains (Figure 2—source data 1), we hypothesized that the elevated expression of Usf1 in the BALB suppressor strain is likely the cause of Clock suppression.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section with reference to source data.

claim: Two independent Usf1 transgenic lines exhibited a significant behavioral period-shortening effect in ClockΔ19/+ animals.
source: From previous work (Hong et al., 2007), we observed that a transgene fused to DNA fragments containing a CMV minimal promoter is induced at low levels, and thus created two independent Usf1 transgenic lines, both of which exhibited a significant behavioral period-shortening effect in ClockΔ19/+ animals, thereby minimizing the possibility of transgene position effects (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 4A showing behavioral data.

claim: The transgenic lines mimic the increase in Usf1 levels observed in the BALB suppressor strain.
source: Quantitation of Usf1 expression confirmed that the transgenic lines mimic the increase in Usf1 levels observed in the BALB suppressor strain (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 4B showing expression data.

claim: Usf1 is the gene encoded by the Soc locus.
source: Based on these results, we conclude that Usf1 is the gene encoded by the Soc locus.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the transgenic rescue experiments.

claim: Usf1 knockout animals do not show changes in period length.
source: Consistent with the dominant action of Soc, Usf1 knockout animals do not show changes in period length, but do exhibit a reduction in circadian amplitude and locomotor activity levels (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 4C,D showing behavioral data.

claim: Usf1 knockout animals exhibit a reduction in circadian amplitude and locomotor activity levels.
source: Consistent with the dominant action of Soc, Usf1 knockout animals do not show changes in period length, but do exhibit a reduction in circadian amplitude and locomotor activity levels (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 4C,D showing behavioral data.

claim: The Usf1 expression difference between B6 and BALB is the result of polymorphisms in a cis-regulatory element causing allele-specific up-regulated expression of the BALB Usf1 transcript.
source: Using three independent methods (Figure 5A,B,C), we found that the Usf1 expression difference between B6 and BALB is the result of polymorphisms in a cis-regulatory element causing allele-specific up-regulated expression of the BALB Usf1 transcript.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figures 5A, 5B, and 5C showing allele-specific expression analysis.

claim: The BALB Usf1 promoter sequence resulted in a significantly higher luciferase signal than that from B6.
source: Although both the B6 and BALB sequences activated the luciferase reporter, the BALB sequence resulted in a significantly higher signal than that from B6 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 5D showing promoter assays.

claim: Seven common polymorphisms (five SNPs and two deletions) match the phenotypic distribution of 16 mouse strains.
source: By exchanging EcoRI-XhoI fragments between the B6 and BALB reporter clones, we narrowed the critical polymorphisms to the EcoRI-XhoI fragment (∼1000 bp) and identified seven common polymorphisms (five SNPs and two deletions) that match the phenotypic distribution of 16 mouse strains (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 5E showing SNP distribution.

claim: Only SNPs 3 and 7 showed strong promoter activity and statistically higher activity from the BALB allele compared to the B6 allele.
source: Among the six fragments tested (SNPs 5 and 6 were contained within the same fragment), only two (SNPs 3 and 7) showed strong promoter activity and statistically higher activity from the BALB allele compared to the B6 allele (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 5F showing promoter assays.

claim: CLOCK and USF1 can bind to common E-boxes in three circadian genes (Dbp, Per2 and Per1).
source: Using chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) followed by qPCR analysis, we verified that CLOCK and USF1 can bind to common E-boxes in three circadian genes (Dbp, Per2 and Per1) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 6A showing ChIP-qPCR data.

claim: In ClockΔ19 mutants, USF1 occupancy increases and CLOCKΔ19 occupancy decreases at E-box sites despite elevated CLOCKΔ19 mutant protein levels.
source: In ClockΔ19 mutants, however, USF1 occupancy increases and CLOCKΔ19 occupancy decreases at these sites despite elevated CLOCKΔ19 mutant protein levels (Figure 6B; Yoshitane et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 6B showing western blot data.

claim: USF1 exhibits a time-dependent DNA binding pattern with a peak at night that is antiphase to that of CLOCK which peaks at ZT8.
source: Further, we observed a time-dependent DNA binding pattern of USF1 with a peak at night that is antiphase to that of CLOCK which peaks at ZT8 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 6C showing time-course ChIP data.

claim: Wild-type CLOCK:BMAL1 complexes bind primarily as a tandem complex (CB2) at all four E-box sites examined.
source: Interestingly, wild-type CLOCK:BMAL1 complexes bind primarily as a tandem complex (CB2) at all four E-box sites with the Dbp EP and Per2 E′ E-boxes showing the most bias towards tandem binding (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 6D showing EMSA data.

claim: The mutant CLOCKΔ19:BMAL1 heterodimer binds primarily as a single complex (CB1) at all four E-box sites.
source: By contrast, the mutant CLOCKΔ19:BMAL1 heterodimer binds primarily as a single complex (CB1) at all four sites.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section based on EMSA analysis.

claim: Kd values of wild-type CLOCK:BMAL1 range from 0.86 nM for Dbp EI2 to 19 nM for Per1 EP1.
source: Although the affinity varies depending on the specific site, Kd values of wild-type CLOCK:BMAL1 range from 0.86 nM for Dbp EI2 to 19 nM for Per1 EP1, while the Kd of CLOCKΔ19:BMAL1 ranges from 9 to 48 nM for Dbp EI2 and Per1 EP1, respectively (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Table 3 showing binding affinity data.

claim: The Kd of CLOCKΔ19:BMAL1 ranges from 9 to 48 nM for Dbp EI2 and Per1 EP1, respectively.
source: Although the affinity varies depending on the specific site, Kd values of wild-type CLOCK:BMAL1 range from 0.86 nM for Dbp EI2 to 19 nM for Per1 EP1, while the Kd of CLOCKΔ19:BMAL1 ranges from 9 to 48 nM for Dbp EI2 and Per1 EP1, respectively (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Table 3 showing binding affinity data.

claim: Kd estimates indicate a binding affinity change from 2.5- to 11.8-fold between wild-type and mutant CLOCK:BMAL1 complexes depending on the E-box site.
source: Kd estimates indicate a binding affinity change from 2.5- to 11.8-fold between wild-type and mutant CLOCK:BMAL1 complexes depending on the E-box site (Figure 7B; Table 3).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 7B and Table 3.

claim: There is no significant difference in USF1 binding affinity between wild-type and ClockΔ19/ClockΔ19 genotypes.
source: There is no significant difference in USF1 binding affinity between the two genotypes and, in fact, the Kd of USF1 is similar to the mutant CLOCKΔ19:BMAL1 complex (Figure 7B; Table 3).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 7B and Table 3.

claim: The Kd of USF1 is similar to the mutant CLOCKΔ19:BMAL1 complex.
source: There is no significant difference in USF1 binding affinity between the two genotypes and, in fact, the Kd of USF1 is similar to the mutant CLOCKΔ19:BMAL1 complex (Figure 7B; Table 3).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 7B and Table 3.

claim: The affinity of the mutant CLOCKΔ19:BMAL1 complex is lower for two reasons: it does not preferentially bind as a tandem complex, and its affinity, even as a tandem complex, remains lower.
source: This suggests that the affinity of the mutant CLOCKΔ19:BMAL1 complex is lower for two reasons: first, it does not preferentially bind as a tandem complex, thus binding may not be cooperative; and second, its affinity, even as a tandem complex, remains lower suggesting that the ClockΔ19 mutation interferes both with cooperativity and with affinity.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the EMSA data.

claim: In wild-type mice, 497 of 1885 USF1 peaks bind either CLOCK or BMAL1.
source: Analysis of USF1 and CLOCK:BMAL1 binding sites reveals extensive overlap in binding in wild-type mice, with 497 of 1885 USF1 peaks binding either CLOCK or BMAL1 (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 8A showing ChIP-Seq analysis.

claim: In ClockΔ19/ClockΔ19 animals, the overlap between USF1 and CLOCK:BMAL1 binding sites increases to 1916 sites, an almost fourfold increase compared to wild-type controls.
source: As predicted for ClockΔ19/ClockΔ19 animals, the overlap between USF1 and CLOCK:BMAL1 binding sites increases significantly to 1916 sites, an almost fourfold increase compared to wild-type controls (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 8A showing ChIP-Seq analysis.

claim: In ClockΔ19/ClockΔ19 mutant animals, USF1 co-occupies 38% of CLOCK:BMAL1 sites (1916/5072)—a dramatic increase from 14% (497/3412) observed in wild-type animals.
source: In ClockΔ19/ClockΔ19 mutant animals, USF1 co-occupies 38% of CLOCK:BMAL1 sites (1916/5072)—a dramatic increase from 14% (497/3412) observed in wild-type animals.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section based on ChIP-Seq analysis.

claim: USF1 binding increases globally in homozygous ClockΔ19 animals, even at sites that do not bind CLOCK or BMAL1, from 1885 peaks in wild-type animals to 6091 peaks in ClockΔ19/ClockΔ19 mutant animals.
source: Surprisingly, USF1 binding also increases globally in homozygous ClockΔ19 animals, even at sites that do not bind CLOCK or BMAL1, from 1885 peaks in wild-type animals to 6091 peaks in ClockΔ19/ClockΔ19 mutant animals.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section based on ChIP-Seq analysis.

claim: Motif analysis of each group of binding sites identified the canonical E-box binding site, CACGTG, as the most significant motif.
source: Motif analysis of each group of binding sites identified the canonical E-box binding site, CACGTG, as the most significant motif, indicating both USF1 and CLOCK:BMAL1 bind to the same consensus sequence in both wild-type and ClockΔ19/ClockΔ19 mice (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 8D showing motif analysis.

claim: Of 41 E-box sites in 15 'reference clock genes', 23 bound USF1 with a significant increase in USF1 binding in the ClockΔ19/ClockΔ19 animals.
source: Of these 41 sites, 23 bound USF1 with a significant increase in USF1 binding in the ClockΔ19/ClockΔ19 animals (Figure 8F,G).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figures 8F and 8G showing ChIP-Seq analysis.

claim: USF1 binds to a majority of reference clock genes and its occupancy on these sites increases in the ClockΔ19/ClockΔ19 mice.
source: Thus, USF1 binds to a majority of reference clock genes and its occupancy on these sites increases in the ClockΔ19/ClockΔ19 mice.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on ChIP-Seq analysis of reference clock genes.

claim: USF1 acts as a partial agonist whose transcriptional regulation of circadian genes can compensate for the reduction in transcriptional activation by the CLOCKΔ19:BMAL1 complex.
source: We propose that USF1 acts as a partial agonist whose transcriptional regulation of circadian genes can compensate for the reduction in transcriptional activation by the CLOCKΔ19:BMAL1 complex.
evidence: This is stated as a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: USF1 is ubiquitously expressed in both mouse and human.
source: USF1 is ubiquitously expressed in both mouse and human and is a member of the evolutionarily conserved bHLH-Zip transcription factor family.
evidence: This is stated directly in the discussion section.

claim: USF1 is a member of the evolutionarily conserved bHLH-Zip transcription factor family.
source: USF1 is ubiquitously expressed in both mouse and human and is a member of the evolutionarily conserved bHLH-Zip transcription factor family.
evidence: This is stated directly in the discussion section.

claim: USF1 participates in the regulation of several processes including lipid and carbohydrate metabolism, immune responses, and the cell cycle.
source: USF1 participates in the regulation of several processes including lipid and carbohydrate metabolism, immune responses, and the cell cycle (Corre and Galibert, 2005).
evidence: This is stated directly in the discussion section with a citation to previous work.

claim: The 40% increase in USF1 levels observed in the Clock suppressor strain could lead to a substantial increase in DNA binding if those levels are below the Kd for USF1 binding.
source: Because USF1 binds as a dimer, the 40% increase in USF1 levels observed in the Clock suppressor strain could lead to a substantial increase in DNA binding if those levels are below the Kd for USF1 binding.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the discussion section.

claim: A modest increase in USF1 could activate target genes more effectively than CLOCKΔ19:BMAL1 because the PER:CRY negative feedback complex cannot repress USF1-mediated transactivation.
source: In addition, because the PER:CRY negative feedback complex cannot repress USF1-mediated transactivation (Figure 3B), a modest increase in USF1 could activate target genes more effectively than CLOCKΔ19:BMAL1.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the discussion section based on experimental data.

claim: As CLOCK:BMAL1 DNA binding decreases at night, USF1 occupancy increases at these sites, exhibiting an antiphase temporal DNA binding pattern.
source: We have found that as CLOCK:BMAL1 DNA binding decreases at night (Rey et al., 2011; Koike et al., 2012), USF1 occupancy increases at these sites, exhibiting an antiphase temporal DNA binding pattern (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the discussion section and supported by Figure 6C.

claim: The role of USF1 at CLOCK:BMAL1 sites could be to maintain an open chromatin state to facilitate CLOCK:BMAL1 binding on the following circadian cycle.
source: We speculate that the role of USF1 at CLOCK:BMAL1 sites could be to maintain an open chromatin state to facilitate CLOCK:BMAL1 binding on the following circadian cycle although additional work would be required to test this hypothesis.
evidence: This is stated as speculation in the discussion section.

claim: In Usf1 knockout mice, a reduction in circadian amplitude and activity levels shows that USF1 plays a role under normal conditions to enhance circadian rhythmicity and robustness.
source: In addition, in Usf1 knockout mice, we observe a reduction in circadian amplitude and activity levels showing that USF1 plays a role under normal conditions to enhance circadian rhythmicity and robustness.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the discussion section based on knockout data.

claim: CLOCK and BMAL1 heterodimerize and initiate transcription of the Period (Per1, Per2) and Cryptochrome (Cry1, Cry2) genes through E-box regulatory sequences.
source: Two members of the bHLH-PAS transcription factor family, CLOCK (and its paralog NPAS2) and BMAL1 (ARNTL), heterodimerize and initiate transcription of the Period (Per1, Per2) and Cryptochrome (Cry1, Cry2) genes through E-box regulatory sequences (King et al., 1997; Gekakis et al., 1998; Hogenesch et al., 1998; Kume et al., 1999; Bunger et al., 2000; Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with citations to previous work.

claim: The PER and CRY proteins form multimeric complexes, translocate to the nucleus, and abrogate their own transcription by repressing CLOCK:BMAL1.
source: The resulting PER and CRY proteins form multimeric complexes, translocate to the nucleus, and abrogate their own transcription by repressing CLOCK:BMAL1 (Lee et al., 2001; Koike et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with citations to previous work.

claim: As the PER and CRY proteins are degraded, CLOCK:BMAL1 occupancy increases to initiate a new round of transcription.
source: As the PER and CRY proteins are degraded, CLOCK:BMAL1 occupancy increases to initiate a new round of transcription (Lowrey and Takahashi, 2011; Koike et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with citations to previous work.

claim: The overall clock mechanism depends on additional feedback loops driven by ROR and REV-ERBα/β.
source: While this forms the major feedback loop of the mammalian molecular clock, the overall mechanism also depends on additional feedback loops driven by ROR and REV-ERBα/β (Preitner et al., 2002; Sato et al., 2004; Ueda et al., 2005; Cho et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with citations to previous work.

claim: At least 13 loci in mice affect circadian behavior through complex epistatic interactions.
source: We previously identified at least 13 loci in mice that affect circadian behavior through complex epistatic interactions (Shimomura et al., 2001), indicating that there are other clock-relevant genes in the mammalian genome.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with a citation to previous work.

claim: Variance in circadian behavior observed in the human population may result from polymorphisms in non-core circadian clock genes.
source: By extension, it is possible that the variance in circadian behavior observed in the human population results from polymorphisms in non-core circadian clock genes.
evidence: This is stated as a possibility in the introduction based on inference from mouse studies.

claim: USF1 binds to E-box sequences.
source: Although it has been reported previously that USF1 binds E-box sequences (Ferré-D'Amaré et al., 1994), our finding that, of the seven Soc candidates, only USF1 effects significant transactivation from circadian-relevant E-boxes, provided initial molecular evidence that Usf1 is a candidate for the Soc locus.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: Like CLOCK and BMAL1, USF1 binds to E-box motifs to regulate transcription.
source: Like CLOCK and BMAL1 (Ripperger and Schibler, 2006), USF1 binds to E-box motifs to regulate transcription (Ferré-D'Amaré et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Binding to tandem E-box sites appears to be cooperative.
